# Aneurysm

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Cardiology and angiology > Vascular diseases > Aneurysm*

[Original Article Link](/library/Wh0P1f)

---

## Summary

Aneurysms are typically defined as vascular enlargements with a diameter ≥ 1.5 times that of a normal <u>artery</u>. <u>True aneurysms</u> are arterial enlargements in which all three layers of the vessel wall are weakened and form part of the aneurysmal wall. <u>False aneurysms</u> are extraarterial <u>hematomas</u> contained by surrounding tissues and/or the <u>tunica adventitia</u> that maintain persistent communication with the arterial lumen. <u>Arterial dissections</u> are vascular enlargements caused by the separation of arterial wall layers as blood enters the <u>intima</u>-media space through a tear in the <u>tunica intima</u>. Aneurysms are also differentiated according to their location. This article discusses the etiology and clinical features of cerebral, extracranial carotid, iliac, femoral, popliteal, and <u>ventricular aneurysms</u>. Symptoms generally depend on the location and size of the aneurysm. Management may be medical, surgical, or endovascular, depending on the type of aneurysm, symptoms, and associated complications.




For more specific information on individual types of aneurysms, see “<u>Thoracic aortic aneurysm</u>,” “<u>Abdominal aortic aneurysm</u>,” “<u>Aortic dissection</u>,” “<u>Dissection of the carotid and the vertebral artery</u>,” and “<u>Subarachnoid hemorrhage</u>.”

---

## Overview

### Categories of vascular enlargement




Abnormal vascular enlargement is often generically referred to as an aneurysm, but there are three distinct types of vascular enlargement with different etiologies and management strategies.




| <br>Comparison of <u>true aneurysm</u>, <u>pseudoaneurysm</u>, and <u>arterial dissection</u>  [[1]](/library/qM0Cpg)[[2]](/library/0FWegM0)[[3]](/library/AtWRTM0)<br> |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | True aneurysm | Pseudoaneurysm (<u>false aneurysm</u>) | Arterial dissection |
| Definition | <br>* An abnormally dilated <u>artery</u> that is bound by all three layers of the arterial wall  [[4]](/library/p30Ljf)<br><br> | <br>* An extravascular <u>hematoma</u> adjacent to an injured arterial wall with a persistent communication with the arterial lumen  [[1]](/library/qM0Cpg)[[4]](/library/p30Ljf)<br><br> | <br>* Separation of the layers of the vascular wall (typically, separation of the <u>tunica intima</u> from the <u>tunica media</u>) by a <u>hematoma</u>  [[5]](/library/YFWngM0)<br><br> |
| Common etiologies and <u>risk factors</u> | <br><br>* <u>Atherosclerosis</u><br><br>* <u>Hypertension</u> [[4]](/library/p30Ljf)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Trauma, e.g., deceleration injury, gunshot<br><br>* <u>Iatrogenic</u> injury, e.g., vascular puncture, cardiovascular <u>surgery</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Hypertension</u><br><br>* Trauma<br><br>* <u>Connective tissue diseases</u>, e.g., <u>Ehlers-Danlos syndrome</u> and <u>Marfan syndrome</u><br><br><br> |
| Pathophysiology | <br>* Inflammation and proteolytic degeneration of <u>connective tissue</u> <u>proteins</u> lead to: [[4]](/library/p30Ljf)<br><br>* Loss of structural integrity of the vessel wall<br><br>* Widening of the vessel<br><br>* Possible <u>intravascular</u> <u>thrombus formation</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Perforation of the vascular wall leads to:<br><br>* Bleeding into the surrounding tissue<br><br>* Formation of an organized extravascular <u>hematoma</u><br><br>* Formation of a communication between a false vascular wall and the true arterial lumen<br><br>* Deceleration injury from <u>blunt trauma</u> typically tears the <u>thoracic aorta</u> <u>distal</u> to the <u>left subclavian artery</u>. [[6]](/library/dFWoSM0)<br><br><br> | <br>* Transverse tear in the arterial <u>intima</u> leads to:<br><br>* Blood entering the <u>intima</u>-media space (creating a false lumen)<br><br>* Formation of a <u>hematoma</u> that continues to propagate within the vascular wall<br><br>* Potential rupture and/or occlusion of branching vessels, with <u>ischemia</u> in the affected areas, due to rising pressure in the aortic wall<br><br> |
| Clinical features | <br>* See “Types of aneurysm by location.”<br><br> | <br><br>* Peripheral <u>pseudoaneurysms</u><br><br>* Painful and pulsatile mass at the site of trauma<br><br>* <u>Thrill</u><br><br>* <u>Bruit</u> on <u>auscultation</u><br><br>* <u>Left ventricular</u> <u>pseudoaneurysms</u> [[7]](/library/2FWThM0)<br><br>* <u>Clinical features of heart failure</u><br><br>* <u>Chest pain</u> and/or <u>dyspnea</u><br><br>* <u>Arrhythmias</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Depends on the location<br><br>* <u>Aortic dissection</u>: tearing or ripping <u>chest pain</u> with neurological features or <u>syncope</u><br><br>* <u>Carotid or vertebral artery dissection</u>: See “<u>Clinical features of stroke by affected vessel</u>” and “<u>Signs of cervical artery dissection</u>.”<br><br><br> |
| Management | <br><br>* Depends on the location, size, growth rate, and presence of complications<br><br>* Options include medical <u>management of ASCVD</u> and open or endovascular <u>stenting</u>, grafting, or repair.<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Depends on the location, size, and presence of complications<br><br>* <u>Femoral artery pseudoaneurysm</u>: Options include <u>conservative management</u>, <u>ultrasound-guided thrombin injection</u>, and surgical or endovascular repair.<br><br>* <u>LV pseudoaneurysm</u>: urgent surgical repair<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Depends on the location and dissection characteristics<br><br>* <u>Aortic dissection</u>: Options include blood pressure management, endovascular repair, and open repair.<br><br>* <u>Carotid or vertebral artery dissection</u>: Options include <u>antithrombotic therapy</u>, endovascular <u>stenting</u>, and open repair.<br><br><br> |





> [!WARNING]
> All three types of vascular enlargement can rupture and cause life-threatening hemorrhage.

| Types of aneurysms by location |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Type | Location | Etiology | Clinical features | Management |
| <u>Thoracic aortic aneurysm</u> (<u>TAA</u>) | <br><br>* <u>Aortic arch</u><br><br>* <u>Ascending aorta</u><br><br>* <u>Descending aorta</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Atherosclerosis</u><br><br>* Trauma<br><br>* <u>Connective tissue diseases</u>, e.g., <u>Ehlers-Danlos syndrome</u> and <u>Marfan syndrome</u><br><br>* <u>Aortitis</u> due to autoimmune disease (e.g., <u>vasculitis</u>, <u>rheumatoid arthritis</u>) or infection (e.g., <u>cardiovascular syphilis</u>)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Usually asymptomatic<br><br>* Feeling of pressure in the chest<br><br>* Thoracic <u>back pain</u><br><br>* Features of <u>aortic regurgitation</u><br><br><br> | <br>* See “<u>Acute management checklist for TAA</u>.”<br><br> |
| <u>Abdominal aortic aneurysm</u> (<u>AAA</u>) | <br>* Infrarenal (most common)   or suprarenal aorta<br><br> | <br><br>* Usually asymptomatic<br><br>* Pulsatile abdominal mass<br><br>* <u>Bruit</u> on <u>auscultation</u><br><br><br> | <br>* See “<u>Acute management checklist for AAA</u>.”<br><br> |  |
| Coronary artery aneurysm | <br><br>* Right (most common) [[8]](/library/7uW4sM0)<br><br>* <u>Left anterior descending</u><br><br>* Left circumflex<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Kawasaki disease</u><br><br>* <u>Polyarteritis nodosa</u><br><br>* <u>Iatrogenic</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Abdominal <u>pain</u><br><br>* <u>Vomiting</u><br><br>* <u>Angina</u><br><br><br> | <br>* Options include medical management, <u>surgery</u> (excision or <u>CABG</u>), and <u>PCI</u>. [[9]](/library/gFWFhM0)<br><br> |
| <u>Cerebral aneurysm</u> | <br><br>* <u>Circle of Willis</u><br><br>* <u>Internal carotid artery</u><br><br><br> | <br>* Depends on the type of aneurysm<br><br> | <br><br>* Usually asymptomatic<br><br>* <u>Mass effects</u><br><br>* In patients with rupture: <u>subarachnoid hemorrhage</u> (<u>SAH</u>)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* See “<u>Acute management checklist for SAH</u>.”<br><br>* See “Treatment” in “<u>Cerebral aneurysm</u>.”<br><br><br> |
| <u>Ventricular aneurysm</u> | <br>* <u>Anterior</u> or apical walls of the <u>left ventricle</u> (most common) [[10]](/library/IsWYw50)<br><br> | <br>* <u>Myocardial infarction</u> (<u>MI</u>)<br><br> | <br><br>* Enlarged <u>heart</u><br><br>* <u>3<sup>rd</sup> heart sound</u>, <u>4<sup>th</sup> heart sound</u><br><br>* Systolic <u>murmur</u><br><br><br> | <br>* See “Treatment” in “<u>Ventricular aneurysm</u>.”<br><br> |
| <u>Ventricular pseudoaneurysm</u> | <br>* <u>Lateral</u> or <u>posterior</u> walls of the <u>left ventricle</u><br><br> | <br>* Urgent <u>surgery</u><br><br> |  |  |
| <u>Popliteal artery aneurysm</u> | <br>* <u>Popliteal artery</u><br><br> | <br>* Multifactorial (i.e., inflammatory, immune, genetic, and mechanical components)<br><br> | <br><br>* Usually asymptomatic mass in the <u>popliteal fossa</u> (bilateral in 50% of patients)<br><br>* <u>Knee pain</u><br><br>* <u>Acute limb ischemia</u> (<u>6 Ps</u>)<br><br><br> | <br>* See “Treatment” in “<u>Popliteal artery aneurysm</u>.”<br><br> |
| <u>Iliac artery aneurysm</u> (<u>IAA</u>) | <br>* <u>Iliac artery</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Atherosclerosis</u><br><br> | <br><br>* May be asymptomatic<br><br>* <u>Acute limb ischemia</u> (<u>6 Ps</u>) from <u>thromboembolism</u><br><br>* Compressive features, e.g., GI obstruction, GU obstruction, nerve palsies<br><br><br> | <br>* See “Treatment” in “<u>IAA</u>.”<br><br> |
| <u>Femoral artery aneurysm</u> (FAA) | <br>* <u>Femoral artery</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Atherosclerosis</u><br><br> | <br><br>* May be asymptomatic<br><br>* Palpable pulsatile mass<br><br>* Compressive or thromboembolic features<br><br><br> | <br>* See “Treatment” in “FAA.”<br><br> |
| <u>Femoral artery pseudoaneurysm</u> | <br>* <u>Femoral artery</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Femoral artery</u> cannulation<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Pain out of proportion</u><br><br>* Palpable pulsatile mass<br><br>* <u>Bruit</u> or <u>thrill</u><br><br>* Compressive or thromboembolic features<br><br><br> | <br>* See “Treatment” in “<u>Femoral artery pseudoaneurysm</u>.”<br><br> |
| <u>Extracranial carotid artery aneurysm</u> | <br><br>* <u>Internal carotid artery</u> (most common) [[11]](/library/GuWBsM0)<br><br>* <u>Common carotid artery</u><br><br>* <u>External carotid artery</u><br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Atherosclerosis</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Pulsatile neck mass<br><br>* <u>Bruit</u><br><br>* <u>Transient ischemic attacks</u> (<u>TIAs</u>) or <u>stroke</u><br><br><br> | <br>* Open surgical or endovascular repair<br><br> |

| Types of arterial dissections by location |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Type | Location | Etiology | Clinical features | Management |
| <u>Aortic dissection</u> | <br><br>* <u>Ascending aorta</u> (<u>Stanford A dissection</u>)<br><br>* <u>Descending aorta</u> (<u>Stanford B dissection</u>)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Hypertension</u><br><br>* Trauma<br><br>* <u>Connective tissue diseases</u>, e.g., <u>Ehlers-Danlos syndrome</u> and <u>Marfan syndrome</u><br><br>* <u>Vasculitis</u><br><br>* Stimulant use<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Sudden and severe tearing or ripping <u>pain</u> in the <u>anterior</u> chest, interscapular area, neck, <u>jaw</u>, or abdomen, depending on the site of dissection<br><br>* <u>Syncope</u><br><br>* Asymmetrical <u>pulse</u> and BP readings<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Control <u>hypertension</u> (<u>Stanford B dissections</u> are generally <u>treated conservatively</u>).<br><br>* Open or endovascular <u>stenting</u>, grafting, or repair (<u>Stanford A dissections</u> require immediate <u>surgery</u>)<br><br>* See “<u>Definitive treatment of aortic dissection</u>” for details.<br><br><br> |
| <u>Carotid artery dissection</u> | <br>* <u>Internal carotid artery</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Trauma<br><br>* <u>Connective tissue diseases</u>, e.g., <u>Ehlers-Danlos syndrome</u> and <u>Marfan syndrome</u><br><br>* <u>Fibromuscular dysplasia</u><br><br>* <u>Hypertension</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Ipsilateral</u> <u>headache</u><br><br>* <u>Pulse</u>-synchronous <u>tinnitus</u><br><br>* <u>Stroke</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Anticoagulation<br><br>* <u>Angioplasty</u>/<u>stenting</u> or surgical intervention<br><br>* See “<u>Cervical artery dissection</u>” for details.<br><br><br> |
| <u>Vertebral artery dissection</u> | <br>* <u>Vertebral arteries</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Occipital <u>headache</u><br><br>* <u>Stroke</u> resembling <u>Wallenberg syndrome</u><br><br><br> |  |  |

## Intracranial aneurysms

### Types




* Saccular aneurysm (<u>Berry aneurysm</u>)  [[12]](/library/vDbATD)

* Round, saccular shape

* Most common type of <u>cerebral aneurysm</u>

* Typically occur at vessel junctions in the <u>circle of Willis</u>, most commonly between the <u>anterior communicating artery</u> and <u>anterior cerebral artery</u>

* Account for ∼ 80% of cases of nontraumatic <u>subarachnoid hemorrhage</u> [[13]](/library/9UcN2b0)

* <u>Risk factors</u> [[14]](/library/FDbgTD)[[15]](/library/EDb8TD)[[16]](/library/mFWViM0)

* Congenital conditions: <u>autosomal-dominant polycystic kidney disease</u>, <u>Ehlers-Danlos syndrome</u>, <u>Marfan syndrome</u>, <u>aortic coarctation</u>

* <u>Hypertension</u>

* Smoking

* African-American race

* Older age

* <u>Hyperlipidemia</u>

* <u>Excessive alcohol consumption</u>

* <u>Family history</u> of aneurysms

* <u>Estrogen deficiency</u> [[17]](/library/5FWiiM0)

* Fusiform aneurysm [[18]](/library/yDbdSD)[[19]](/library/NFW-RM0)

* Dilation of the entire circumference of the <u>artery</u>

* Most frequently occur in the vertebrobasilar system

* Associated with <u>connective tissue diseases</u> and <u>atherosclerosis</u>

* Mycotic aneurysm [[20]](/library/BDbzgD)

* Mushroom-shaped dilation of infected vessel walls

* Caused by <u>septic emboli</u> (mostly due to bacterial <u>endocarditis</u>)

* Occur at small, peripheral segments of cerebral vessels and often involve the <u>middle cerebral artery</u> [[21]](/library/xDbEgD)

* Traumatic <u>intracranial aneurysm</u> [[22]](/library/CDbqgD)

* Comprise < 1% of all <u>intracranial aneurysms</u>

* Most commonly occur in the supraclinoid <u>internal carotid artery</u> and <u>anterior cerebral artery</u>

* Have a high risk of rupture

* Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysm

* Associated with <u>hypertension</u> and <u>diabetes</u>

* Affect small lenticulostriate vessels in the <u>basal ganglia</u> and <u>thalamus</u>

* Rupture may cause <u>intracerebral hemorrhage</u>.

### Clinical features [[23]](/library/oFW0QM0)[[24]](/library/LFWwiM0)




* Usually asymptomatic

* <u>Headache</u>  [[25]](/library/qFWCQM0)

* <u>Signs and symptoms of TIA</u> [[26]](/library/e9cxme0)

* <u>Mass effects</u> (symptoms depend on the affected vessel) 

* <u>Anterior communicating artery</u>: <u>bitemporal hemianopia</u>, <u>visual acuity</u> defects (<u>optic nerve palsy</u> from compression of <u>CN II</u> at the <u>optic chiasm</u>)

* <u>Posterior communicating artery</u>: <u>mydriasis</u> (<u>CN III</u> palsy from compression of <u>parasympathetic</u> fibers); <u>ptosis</u> and <u>ophthalmoplegia</u> in severe compression

* Intracavernous <u>internal carotid artery</u>: <u>CN III palsy</u>, <u>CN IV palsy</u>, <u>CN V palsy</u>, and <u>CN VI palsy</u> [[27]](/library/IFWYjM0)[[28]](/library/rFWfjM0)

* <u>Clinical features of SAH</u> (if aneurysm ruptures)





### Diagnostics [[26]](/library/e9cxme0)[[29]](/library/OsWIE50)




<u>Cerebral aneurysms</u> are often found incidentally during the workup of suspected <u>intracranial hemorrhage</u> (e.g., <u>SAH</u>, <u>ICH</u>), <u>ischemic stroke</u>, or other <u>CNS</u> lesion.




* Unruptured aneurysm (incidental finding on noncontrast <u>neuroimaging</u> or suspected clinically): Obtain <u>neuroimaging</u> with <u>angiography</u>. [[26]](/library/e9cxme0)

* <u>CTA</u> head or <u>MRA</u> head: first-line option (high <u>sensitivity</u>, noninvasive)

* <u>Digital subtraction angiography</u> (<u>DSA</u>): <u>gold standard</u> for <u>accuracy</u> , helpful for operative planning, invasive

* Suspected ruptured aneurysm or <u>sentinel leak</u>: Follow the “<u>Diagnostic approach for SAH</u>.”

* Confirmed <u>SAH</u> on plain CT head: Obtain <u>CTA</u> head or <u>catheter arteriography</u>. [[29]](/library/OsWIE50)

* Surveillance of known aneurysm: Options include <u>CTA</u> head, <u>MRA</u> head, and <u>DSA</u>.  [[26]](/library/e9cxme0)[[29]](/library/OsWIE50)

* High-risk asymptomatic individuals (e.g., strong <u>family history</u>, <u>Ehlers-Danlos syndrome</u>, <u>polycystic kidney disease</u>): Consider screening with <u>CTA</u> head or <u>MRA</u> head.  [[26]](/library/e9cxme0)[[30]](/library/oaa0lQ)[[31]](/library/GFYBjI)





> [!TIP]
> <u>Angiography</u> (e.g., <u>CTA</u>, <u>MRA</u>, or <u>DSA</u>) helps determine the location, size, and morphology of most <u>cerebral aneurysms</u>, but visualization of <u>Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms</u> may not be possible with standard techniques.

### Differential diagnoses




* Other cerebrovascular lesion: e.g., <u>arteriovenous malformations</u>, <u>fibromuscular dysplasia</u>

* <u>Brain tumor</u>: e.g., <u>pituitary adenoma</u>, <u>meningioma</u>, intracranial <u>metastasis</u>

* <u>Brain abscess</u>

* <u>Stroke</u>: See “<u>Overview of stroke</u>.”

* <u>Ischemic stroke</u>: See “<u>Stroke symptoms by affected vessel</u>.”

* <u>Hemorrhagic stroke</u>: See “<u>Differential diagnosis of intracranial hemorrhage</u>.”

* Other causes of <u>cranial nerve palsies</u>

* Other causes of <u>headache</u>: See “<u>Differential diagnosis of headache</u>.”





### Treatment




#### Unruptured <u>intracranial aneurysms</u> [[26]](/library/e9cxme0)[[32]](/library/BFWz4M0)




Treatment depends on the aneurysm size, location, growth rate, and the patient's <u>perioperative risk assessment</u>.  [[26]](/library/e9cxme0)




* Interventional management [[32]](/library/BFWz4M0)

* Surgical <u>clipping</u>

* <u>Endovascular coiling</u>

* See “<u>Intracranial aneurysm repair</u>” for details.

* <u>Conservative management</u>

* <u>Primary prevention of ASCVD</u> and surveillance imaging (e.g., <u>CTA</u>, <u>MRA</u>) [[29]](/library/OsWIE50)[[32]](/library/BFWz4M0)

* Consider for low-risk lesions, older patients, and patients with comorbidities. [[26]](/library/e9cxme0)[[33]](/library/yFWdkM0)





![Clipped intracranial aneurysm](media/w0tmjw5r36bz7z6k1skobjqm.jpg)

Clipped intracranial aneurysm

![Intracranial aneurysm with coil embolization](media/uw83i2gxs5e8dmrsudsxmpx5.jpg)

Intracranial aneurysm with coil embolization




#### Ruptured aneurysms




* <u>Subarachnoid hemorrhage</u> (most common): See “<u>Management of SAH</u>.”

* <u>Intracerebral hemorrhage</u> (rare): See “<u>Intracerebral hemorrhage management</u>.”

## Ventricular aneurysm

### Definition [[10]](/library/IsWYw50)




<u>Ventricular aneurysm</u> is a focal enlargement and/or bulge in the ventricle caused by thinning of the <u>myocardium</u>.




### Etiology




* <u>Myocardial infarction</u> (most common) [[35]](/library/c8WalM0)

* Occurs in < 5% of patients after <u>MI</u>  [[36]](/library/tbYXvn)

* Typically occurs within 2 weeks of <u>MI</u> but can occur months later [[37]](/library/usWp950)

* <u>Risk factors</u> include:

* Occlusion of the <u>left anterior descending</u> <u>coronary artery</u>  [[10]](/library/IsWYw50)

* Female sex [[38]](/library/ZOXZIy)





### Clinical features




* Enlarged <u>heart</u> on percussion

* Diffuse and displaced apical <u>pulse</u> to the left <u>midclavicular line</u>

* 3<sup>rd</sup> and <u>4<sup>th</sup> heart sounds</u>

* Systolic <u>murmur</u> (<u>mitral regurgitation</u>)   [[39]](/library/o8W0nM0)





![Mitral Regurgitation (MR) - Heart Auscultation - Episode 4](media/small_6009e71c49202.jpg)

Mitral Regurgitation (MR) - Heart Auscultation - Episode 4




### Diagnosis




* ECG findings of LV aneurysm

* Similar to <u>ECG findings of STEMI</u> or other causes of <u>ST elevation</u>

* Features favoring the diagnosis of <u>LV aneurysm</u>

* Persistent <u>ST elevation</u> (> 2 weeks), most often in the <u>anterior</u> <u>precordial leads</u> (classic finding)  [[40]](/library/GsWBw50)

* Combined T/QRS <u>ratio</u> of leads V1–V4 of < 0.22  [[41]](/library/tsWX950)

* Single T/QRS <u>ratio</u> of any one <u>anterior</u> <u>precordial lead</u> (V1, V2, V3, or V4) of ≤ 0.36 [[42]](/library/clXaDy)

* <u>CXR</u>: <u>cardiomegaly</u>, bulge on the left side of the <u>heart</u> [[37]](/library/usWp950)[[43]](/library/b8WHOM0)

* <u>Echocardiography</u>: dyskinetic wall motion and <u>diastolic</u> deformity [[10]](/library/IsWYw50)

* <u>Cardiac CT</u> or <u>cardiac MRI</u>: can identify wall abnormalities not seen on <u>echocardiography</u> [[43]](/library/b8WHOM0)[[44]](/library/7sW4w50)

* <u>Ventriculography</u>: <u>gold standard</u> for distinguishing between <u>LV aneurysm</u> and <u>LV pseudoaneurysm</u> (invasive) [[44]](/library/7sW4w50)

* <u>Cardiac biomarkers</u>: Nonspecific elevations may be present.  [[37]](/library/usWp950)





### Treatment [[36]](/library/tbYXvn)[[45]](/library/EM08qg)




#### <u>Conservative management</u>




* Indication: small, asymptomatic aneurysms [[46]](/library/d8WolM0)

* Treatment

* Monitor aneurysm size with serial imaging.

* <u>Manage heart failure</u> if present.

* Anticoagulation if <u>LV thrombus</u> is present [[47]](/library/bpWHLm0)





#### <u>Surgery</u> [[10]](/library/IsWYw50)[[46]](/library/d8WolM0)




* Indications

* Large size or continued expansion

* Refractory <u>heart failure</u>, <u>arrhythmia</u>, or <u>thromboembolism</u>

* <u>Pseudoaneurysm</u>

* Technique: aneurysmectomy (often in conjunction with <u>coronary artery revascularization</u>)





### Prevention [[10]](/library/IsWYw50)[[36]](/library/tbYXvn)




* Early reperfusion (e.g., <u>PCI</u>) after acute <u>MI</u>

* Early administration of <u>ACEIs</u> or <u>beta blockers</u> after acute <u>MI</u>





### Complications [[48]](/library/kIYm1q)




* <u>Arrhythmias</u>, e.g., <u>sustained VT</u> in patients with <u>hypertrophic cardiomyopathy</u> [[49]](/library/xBYE17)

* <u>Ventricular free wall rupture</u> and <u>cardiac tamponade</u>

* <u>LV thrombus</u> formation → <u>thromboembolism</u> (e.g., <u>stroke</u>, <u>mesenteric</u> <u>ischemia</u>, <u>renal infarction</u>)

* <u>Heart failure</u>





### <u>LV aneurysm</u> vs. <u>LV pseudoaneurysm</u>




| <br>Comparison of <u>LV aneurysm</u> and <u>LV pseudoaneurysm</u> [[10]](/library/IsWYw50)[[44]](/library/7sW4w50)[[50]](/library/HsWKw50)<br> |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  | <br><u>LV aneurysm</u> <br> | <br><u>LV pseudoaneurysm</u> <br> |
| Description | <br><br>* Thinned ventricular wall (often < 5 mm) [[44]](/library/7sW4w50)<br><br>* Akinetic or dyskinetic wall motion<br><br>* Typically a more benign, stable condition than <u>LV pseudoaneurysm</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Ventricular free wall rupture</u><br><br>* Adherent <u>pericardium</u> contains the resulting <u>hematoma</u><br><br><br> |
| <u>Epidemiology</u> | <br>* More common than <u>LV pseudoaneurysm</u><br><br> | <br>* Rarer than <u>LV aneurysm</u><br><br> |
| Etiology | <br>* Complication of <u>MI</u>; usually occurs within weeks<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>MI</u><br><br>* Cardiac <u>surgery</u> [[35]](/library/c8WalM0)<br><br>* Chest trauma<br><br>* Congenital disease<br><br>* <u>Tumor</u> invasion<br><br><br> |
| Location | <br>* Typically <u>anterior</u> or apical<br><br> | <br>* Typically <u>posterior</u> or <u>lateral</u><br><br> |
| Risk of complications | <br>* Can cause <u>thromboembolism</u> and <u>sudden cardiac death</u> in patients with <u>HCM</u> [[51]](/library/rsWfw50)[[52]](/library/ssWtw50)<br><br> | <br>* High risk of rupture, <u>cardiac tamponade</u>, and <u>sudden cardiac death</u><br><br> |
| <u>ECG</u> | <br><br>* Typically persistent <u>ST elevations</u><br><br>* See “<u>ECG findings of LV aneurysms</u>.”<br><br><br> | <br>* Typically nonspecific ST changes [[53]](/library/FsWg950)<br><br> |
| Imaging | <br><br>* Similar appearance on <u>echocardiography</u> [[50]](/library/HsWKw50)<br><br>* Diagnosis may require <u>cardiac MRI</u>, <u>cardiac CT</u>, or <u>ventriculography</u> [[44]](/library/7sW4w50)[[53]](/library/FsWg950)<br><br><br> |  |
| Treatment | <br><br>* Varies based on size and symptoms<br><br>* Options include observation and <u>surgery</u>.<br><br><br> | <br>* Urgent surgical repair<br><br> |





![Left ventricular aneurysm](media/qr4ffpbbljx0u58eo9lii0m8.jpg)

Left ventricular aneurysm

![Left ventricular pseudoaneurysm](media/r7m8d5dw9ql45c65xrigoo3e.jpg)

Left ventricular pseudoaneurysm

## Popliteal artery aneurysm

### <u>Epidemiology</u> [[54]](/library/oM00pg)[[55]](/library/vsWA950)




* <u>Prevalence</u>: second most common aneurysm (after <u>AAA</u>), most common peripheral aneurysm

* <u>♂</u> > <u>♀</u>

* Mean age: 65 years





### Etiology



* Multifactorial (i.e., inflammatory, immune, genetic, and mechanical components)




### Clinical features [[54]](/library/oM00pg)[[55]](/library/vsWA950)




* Most patients present with an asymptomatic mass in the <u>popliteal fossa</u> (bilateral in 50% of cases).

* If symptomatic

* <u>Knee pain</u>

* <u>6 Ps</u> of <u>acute limb ischemia</u>

* Signs and/or symptoms of chronic <u>peripheral artery disease</u>





> [!TIP]
> The symptoms of a <u>popliteal artery aneurysm</u> may be similar to those of atherosclerotic <u>peripheral vascular disease</u>. [[55]](/library/vsWA950)




### Diagnosis [[54]](/library/oM00pg)[[55]](/library/vsWA950)




See also “<u>Acute limb ischemia</u> diagnostics” and “<u>Peripheral artery disease diagnostics</u>.”




* <u>Duplex ultrasound</u>:  (initial test): can identify vascular enlargement, <u>thrombus</u>, and reduced patency; can exclude <u>popliteal cysts</u>

* <u>CTA</u> extremity or <u>MRA</u> extremity: helpful for <u>preoperative assessment</u>

* <u>Digital subtraction angiography</u>: may be required if <u>acute limb ischemia</u> is present  [[55]](/library/vsWA950)





![CT angiography of a popliteal artery aneurysm](media/kgeb8t8dc2jvrqi4tx6b1oz5.jpg)

CT angiography of a popliteal artery aneurysm




### Management [[55]](/library/vsWA950)



* All patients

* Screen for <u>contralateral</u> <u>popliteal artery aneurysm</u> and <u>AAA</u>.

* Risk <u>stratify</u> for <u>acute limb ischemia</u>, e.g., using <u>Rutherford grading</u>.

* Begin <u>management of acute limb ischemia</u>, e.g., anticoagulation, if present.

* Optimize <u>management of ASCVD</u>.




* <u>Surgery</u>

* The decision to repair is multifactorial and depends on aneurysm size, thromboembolic risk, <u>perioperative risk assessment</u>, and the patient's <u>life expectancy</u>.

* Indications include:

* Diameter ≥ 2 cm  [[55]](/library/vsWA950)

* Presence of <u>thrombus</u> and/or suspicion of embolism

* <u>Distal</u> arterial insufficiency

* <u>Conservative management</u>

* Long-term clinical monitoring

* Serial imaging





### Complications [[54]](/library/oM00pg)[[55]](/library/vsWA950)




* <u>Acute limb ischemia</u> and possible loss of limb

* Chronic <u>thrombus</u> and/or <u>distal</u> embolization, e.g., <u>blue toe syndrome</u>

* Rupture (rare)

---

## Iliac artery aneurysm

### <u>Epidemiology</u> [[56]](/library/4GW3z50)[[57]](/library/S8WyNM0)




* <u>Iliac artery</u> aneurysms accompany up to 50% of <u>AAAs</u>  [[58]](/library/EsW8950)

* Rarely occur in isolation





### Etiology [[56]](/library/4GW3z50)[[57]](/library/S8WyNM0)




* Similar to <u>AAAs</u>: See “<u>Risk factors for atherosclerosis</u>.”

* Other causes: infection, <u>collagen vascular disease</u>, trauma, <u>iatrogenic</u> injury  [[59]](/library/OGWIz50)





### Clinical features [[59]](/library/OGWIz50)




* Unruptured <u>IAA</u>

* Usually asymptomatic [[60]](/library/kGWmz50)

* Palpable mass: <u>pelvic</u>, groin, or rectal

* <u>Mass effect</u> caused by compression and/or <u>erosion</u> into adjacent vessels, nerves, or organs [[58]](/library/EsW8950)[[59]](/library/OGWIz50)[[60]](/library/kGWmz50)

* <u>Pain</u>: abdominal, rectal, flank, groin, hip, or leg

* <u>Clinical features of urinary obstruction</u>, features of <u>urosepsis</u> or <u>pyelonephritis</u>

* <u>Constipation</u>, <u>tenesmus</u>, <u>clinical features of bowel obstruction</u>

* Features of <u>acute limb ischemia</u> (i.e., <u>6 Ps</u>), swelling, and/or <u>neuropathic pain</u> in <u>ipsilateral</u> extremity

* Ruptured <u>IAA</u> [[59]](/library/OGWIz50)[[60]](/library/kGWmz50)

* Similar to clinical features of <u>ruptured AAA</u>

* <u>Hemorrhagic shock</u>

* Acute groin <u>pain</u>

* <u>GI bleeding</u> or <u>hematuria</u> (if the aneurysm erodes into adjacent organs)





### Diagnostics [[59]](/library/OGWIz50)[[60]](/library/kGWmz50)[[61]](/library/V30Ghf)




IAAs are often diagnosed incidentally during <u>AAA screening</u> or the workup of abdominal symptoms. [[59]](/library/OGWIz50)




* Abdominal <u>ultrasound</u>: used for screening, initial investigation in symptomatic patients, and surveillance

* <u>CTA</u> or <u>MRA</u> abdomen and <u>pelvis</u>: more accurate than <u>ultrasound</u>; usually required for operative planning





![Iliac artery aneurysm](media/kdmd3v3w50sg0e3hb00zbbm0.jpg)

Iliac artery aneurysm




### Treatment [[56]](/library/4GW3z50)[[62]](/library/uTcpsb0)[[63]](/library/h8WcmM0)




IAAs are usually repaired during treatment for concomitant <u>AAAs</u>. [[61]](/library/V30Ghf)[[64]](/library/4JY38J)[[65]](/library/tGWXaM0)




* Procedure: open surgical or endovascular repair

* Indications

* Symptomatic aneurysm

* Diameter ≥ 3.5 cm

* Rapid expansion

* Concomitant <u>AAA repair</u> planned





### Complications




* Rupture

* <u>Distal</u> embolization, e.g., <u>blue toe syndrome</u>

## Femoral artery aneurysm and pseudoaneurysm

### Overview




| <br><u>Femoral artery aneurysm</u> vs. <u>femoral artery pseudoaneurysm</u> [[66]](/library/xGWEYM0)[[67]](/library/BGWzYM0)[[68]](/library/yGWdbM0)[[69]](/library/_GW5bM0)[[70]](/library/zGWrbM0)<br> |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  | <u>Femoral artery aneurysm</u> | <u>Femoral artery pseudoaneurysm</u> |
| Description | <br>* Dilated vessel surrounded by all three vessel layers<br><br> | <br>* <u>Hematoma</u> bound only by a fibrous membrane outside the <u>artery</u> (<u>pseudocapsule</u>) or by the <u>tunica adventitia</u> [[69]](/library/_GW5bM0)[[70]](/library/zGWrbM0)<br><br> |
| <u>Epidemiology</u> | <br><br>* Second most common peripheral <u>artery</u> aneurysm [[69]](/library/_GW5bM0)<br><br>* <u>♂</u> > <u>♀</u> [[61]](/library/V30Ghf)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Most common site for <u>pseudoaneurysm</u> formation [[1]](/library/qM0Cpg)<br><br>* Occurs in ∼ 1% of patients after <u>iatrogenic</u> <u>femoral artery</u> puncture [[68]](/library/yGWdbM0)<br><br>* <u>♀</u> > <u>♂</u> [[68]](/library/yGWdbM0)<br><br><br> |
| Most common cause | <br>* <u>Atherosclerosis</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Femoral artery</u> cannulation<br><br> |
| Diagnosis | <br><br>* <u>Duplex ultrasonography</u><br><br>* <u>CTA</u> or <u>MRA</u> extremity<br><br><br> |  |
| Management options | <br><br>* Open surgical repair (most common)<br><br>* Endovascular repair or embolization<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Observation<br><br>* <u>Ultrasound-guided thrombin injection</u><br><br>* Surgical repair (selected cases)<br><br><br> |
| Complications | <br><br>* Rupture<br><br>* <u>Thromboembolism</u><br><br>* Infection<br><br>* Compression of adjacent structures<br><br><br> |  |





### Femoral artery aneurysm




#### Etiology [[66]](/library/xGWEYM0)[[69]](/library/_GW5bM0)




* <u>Atherosclerosis</u> is the most common cause.

* <u>Risk factors</u> include <u>ASCVD risk factors</u> (especially male sex).

* Rare causes include <u>vasculitis</u> (e.g., <u>Behcet disease</u>) and trauma.





#### Clinical features [[61]](/library/V30Ghf)[[66]](/library/xGWEYM0)[[69]](/library/_GW5bM0)




* Unruptured

* Asymptomatic in 30–40% of patients [[69]](/library/_GW5bM0)

* Thigh or groin <u>pain</u>

* Palpable pulsatile mass in the thigh

* Compressive and/or thromboembolic features, e.g.:

* Nerve palsy

* <u>Acute limb ischemia</u>

* <u>DVT</u>, <u>phlegmasia cerulea dolens</u>

* Ruptured: severe <u>pain</u>, swelling, <u>ecchymosis</u>, <u>clinical features of shock</u>





#### Diagnostics [[61]](/library/V30Ghf)[[66]](/library/xGWEYM0)




<u>Femoral artery aneurysm</u> is often diagnosed incidentally during the workup of other aneurysms or vascular conditions. [[61]](/library/V30Ghf)




* <u>Duplex ultrasonography</u>

* <u>CTA</u> extremity

* <u>MRA</u> extremity





#### Treatment [[61]](/library/V30Ghf)[[69]](/library/_GW5bM0)[[70]](/library/zGWrbM0)




* All patients

* Begin <u>management of acute limb ischemia</u>, e.g., anticoagulation, if present.

* Optimize <u>management of ASCVD</u>.

* Consider <u>antiplatelet agents</u>. [[61]](/library/V30Ghf)[[71]](/library/N8W-5M0)

* Interventional treatment [[69]](/library/_GW5bM0)

* Indications

* Diameter > 2.5 cm

* Symptomatic aneurysm of any size

* Technique: open surgical repair (most common), endovascular <u>stent</u> placement





#### Complications [[69]](/library/_GW5bM0)




* Rupture

* <u>Thromboembolism</u> and <u>acute limb ischemia</u>

* Infection





### Femoral artery pseudoaneurysm




#### Etiology [[1]](/library/qM0Cpg)[[68]](/library/yGWdbM0)




* Typically caused by <u>femoral artery</u> cannulation (e.g., for <u>cardiac catheterization</u>)

* Procedural <u>risk factors</u> include large sheath size, multiple punctures, and inadequate postprocedure compression.

* Patient <u>risk factors</u> include:

* Female sex

* Older age

* <u>PAD</u>

* <u>Obesity</u>

* <u>Hypertension</u>

* Use of <u>antithrombotic agents</u>





#### Clinical features [[1]](/library/qM0Cpg)




* Postcannulation groin <u>pain</u> (especially <u>pain out of proportion</u> to physical findings)

* Swelling or palpable pulsatile mass

* <u>Bruit</u> or <u>thrill</u>

* Compressive symptoms, e.g.:

* <u>Peripheral neuropathy</u>

* <u>DVT</u>

* <u>Clinical features of PAD</u>





![Pseudoaneurysm of the femoral artery](media/t19p3rnnfs0t18dp91uyjpct.jpg)

Pseudoaneurysm of the femoral artery




#### Diagnostics




Usually obtained because of clinical suspicion after <u>femoral artery</u> cannulation




* <u>Duplex ultrasonography</u> (preferred initial study)  [[1]](/library/qM0Cpg)[[72]](/library/L8WwMM0)

* <u>CTA</u> extremity

* <u>MRA</u> extremity





#### Treatment [[1]](/library/qM0Cpg)[[68]](/library/yGWdbM0)[[70]](/library/zGWrbM0)[[73]](/library/dtWocM0)




* Observation with serial imaging: appropriate for uncomplicated <u>pseudoaneurysms</u> that are < 3 cm and asymptomatic  [[73]](/library/dtWocM0)

* Ultrasound-guided thrombin injection: appropriate for uncomplicated <u>pseudoaneurysms</u> that are ≥ 3 cm or symptomatic, and patients taking <u>anticoagulants</u> [[70]](/library/zGWrbM0)

* <u>Thrombin</u> is injected directly into the cavity of the <u>pseudoaneurysm</u> under <u>ultrasound</u> guidance.

* <u>Thrombin</u> initiates rapid <u>thrombosis</u> and <u>hemostasis</u>.

* <u>Ultrasound</u>-guided manual compression: Compression is applied directly on the neck of the aneurysm for ≥ 20 minutes.  [[73]](/library/dtWocM0)

* Open surgical repair, endovascular repair, and/or embolization is indicated for: [[2]](/library/0FWegM0)[[73]](/library/dtWocM0)

* Rapidly expanding <u>pseudoaneurysms</u>

* Complicated <u>pseudoaneurysms</u>, e.g., associated <u>skin</u> <u>necrosis</u>, <u>cellulitis</u>, <u>acute limb ischemia</u>, previous vascular <u>surgery</u>

* Failure of less invasive therapy





#### Complications [[68]](/library/yGWdbM0)




* Prolonged hospital stay

* Compression of adjacent structures

* Infection

* Rupture

* <u>Thromboembolism</u>





#### Prevention [[1]](/library/qM0Cpg)




* The risk of developing a periprocedural femoral <u>pseudoaneurysm</u> can be reduced by:

* Using <u>fluoroscopy</u> or <u>ultrasound</u> to guide arterial puncture

* Appropriate length of arterial compression after needle or sheath removal, typically ≥ 10 minutes [[74]](/library/-uWDFM0)

* Vascular closure devices reduce the risk of developing a large <u>hematoma</u>, but their <u>effectiveness</u> in preventing <u>pseudoaneurysms</u> is unclear. [[75]](/library/_uW5FM0)[[76]](/library/zuWrFM0)[[77]](/library/m8WVMM0)





> [!WARNING]
> Apply manual pressure over the site of a <u>femoral artery</u> puncture for at least 10 minutes to reduce the risk of <u>pseudoaneurysm</u> formation.
